title: Noise-enhanced temporal boundary states in non-Hermitian systems
authors: Jielong Zhang, Bozheng Xue, Xianfeng Man, Baizhan Xia
abstract: Time-periodic modulation introduces a synthetic degree of freedom to manipulate topological phases. This synthetic dimension can trigger a phase transition that localizes a boundary state at the temporal interface. Noise is widely deemed a fundamental threat to topological protection, universally anticipated to weaken or even destroy topological states. Here, we introduce periodically repeated temporal noise and fully random temporal noise into a 2D periodically driven non-Hermitian system. Paradoxically, under ensemble averaging, such temporal noise drives an exponential enhancement of the response intensity at the temporal interface. An averaged superoperator analysis shows that the noiseless band structure is preserved under both types of noise. Yet the noise increases the growth rate of growing modes while suppressing the decay rate of decaying ones. Finally, we experimentally realize the noise-enhanced temporal boundary state in a robotic metamaterial network. This finding establishes temporal noise as a constructive ingredient, enabling the unambiguous emergence of topological states and conferring exceptional robustness upon topological devices.
summary: The paper demonstrates that temporal noise can paradoxically enhance topological boundary states in non-Hermitian systems. Using both theoretical superoperator analysis and experimental realization in a robotic metamaterial network, the authors show that averaging over noise leads to exponential amplification of these interface states. This establishes noise as a functional tool for engineering robust quantum devices.
main_problem: The study investigates whether temporal noise, typically viewed as a destructive element, can constructively enhance or stabilize topological boundary states in non-Hermitian systems.
main_result: Ensemble averaging over periodic or random temporal noise leads to an exponential enhancement of the response intensity at the temporal interface, establishing noise as a constructive ingredient for robust topological state emergence.
method: The analysis combines theoretical superoperator methods (Floquet theory) with experimental validation using programmable robotic metamaterial networks.
model_or_system: The system is modeled by a 2D periodically driven non-Hermitian tight-binding Hamiltonian, which is experimentally realized in a spring–mass network composed of controllable oscillators.
key_observables: Response intensity at the temporal interface, growth rate of growing modes, decay rate of decaying ones, and quasi-energy spectrum gaps.
important_parameters: Noise strength (W), modulation frequency ($\Omega$), coupling parameters ($\alpha$), and time periodicity ($T$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on ensemble averaging for noise effects and the slowly varying envelope approximation for the continuum model.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate quasi-energy spectra showing gap opening, exponential growth of response intensity under both PRTN and FRTN noise regimes, and schematics/measurements from the robotic metamaterial network demonstrating amplification.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from theoretical analysis using Floquet Hamiltonians to deriving superoperator evolution equations under different noise types (PRTN vs. FRTN), culminating in a detailed experimental realization and measurement campaign on a physical metamaterial platform.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses open quantum systems dynamics by showing how engineered noise can stabilize or amplify coherent quantum phenomena, which is highly relevant for designing robust quantum devices.
